\section{Domain Model}
Figure~\ref{ch5:fig:domain} shows the concepts FlakeTrace works with and how they relate. Each
box uses the name the concept has in the code, shown in brackets. The figure is drawn from the
three contracts in \texttt{docs/contracts/} and from the data classes in \texttt{eval/baseline.py}
and \texttt{runner/diagnose.py}.

A \emph{diagnosis} starts from one failing test, the \emph{victim}, in a Maven project. Member~2's
runner executes \emph{test orders}. Each \emph{run} uses one fresh JVM and runs the tests in
exactly the given order, and every test in the order gets an \emph{outcome}. A failed outcome
carries a \emph{failure signature}: the exception type and a normalised stack trace. The message is
kept but not compared (\texttt{FailureSignature.matches}), because it can change from run to run
for the same bug. The first real failure of the victim becomes the diagnosis's \emph{reference}
signature, and later runs count only failures that match it. Every run is one line of the
\emph{execution record}, and the project's files are hashed before and after the diagnosis
(\emph{source integrity}), because FlakeTrace must not change the code it analyses.

My module adds the explanation. A test makes \emph{accesses} to a \emph{shared resource}, either a
static field or a system property with a constant key, by reading or writing it at a bytecode
location. Each access also records which root it was reached from (for example a \texttt{@Before}
method) and how many calls deep it is. An \emph{edge} pairs one polluter write with one victim read
of the same resource. It is the mechanism the report names. When the runner finds several
polluters, each one is analysed as a separate pair with the victim. Finally, Member~3's
\emph{report} concludes the diagnosis with an outcome and, if it is unresolved, a typed reason.
